newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries mixed at midday; Greenspan calms mkt.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries mixed at midday; Greenspan calms mkt.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities were mixed at midday Tuesday as comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan soothed bond market players.
Prices slumped when initial headlines on portions of Greenspan's speech citing concern over possible wage inflation.
But Greenspan's remarks grew less alarming as they continued. Prices recouped losses with the long bond gaining 11/32 to trade at 96-5/32, yielding 6.80 percent.
The 30-year Treasury bond had been trading almost a full point lower shortly after initial excerpts were reported.

"It's straight stuff he's been talking about for a while. If he's holding any cards in his hand that are different, he's not revealing them," said Matt Alexy, chief market strategist on the trading floor at Credit Suisse First Boston, of Greenspan's remarks.

Alexy noted that the Treasury would auction $23 billion of three- and six-month bills this afternoon. The Treasury will also auction $17.5 billion of two-year notes on Wednesday. Activity was fairly quiet at the front end of the yield curve, he said.

Also bolstering bonds were Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's comments that a strong dollar was in the best interest of the U.S. and he was not concerned about a strong dollar's potential effect on the U.S. trade deficit. Overnight the dollar had hit a 42-month high against the Japanese yen before closing below the 118 level.

Kretzmer said many participants had been shorting positions as a defensive move just in case Greenspan chose to use his appearance before the Senate as a platform to issue a warning on inflation or monetary policy.
"There was a lot of trepidation before the speech, though few players cited any specific reasons. Now many were covering short positions, Kretzmer said.

He noted that Greenspan would be back before Congress for Humphrey-Hawkins testimony in about a month and said the Fed chairman probably was saving any substantive news he wanted to deliver about the economy until then.

Also this session, Treasury announced it would sell $7.0 billion of 10-year inflation-indexed notes on January 29, to settle on February 6. Trade in the inflation-indexed notes started and Rubin said he was unsure about maturities of future such securities.
He said the securities, to be sold on a regular quarterly basis, might boost savings and cut borrowing costs.
The Fed, as expected, intervened in the banking system during its usual time Tuesday, injecting reserves via a round of nine-day fixed system repurchase agreements. Fed funds were at 5-15/16 percent.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 99-7/32, yielding 6.31 percent. Ten-year notes were up 5/32 at 99-25/32, yielding 6.53 percent.
Three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.03 percent. Six-month rates were up 2/32 at 5.09 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.30 percent.
